claims.text: Adding titanium to a high-entropy alloy can improve its hardness.
Adding titanium to a high-entropy alloy can improve its strength.
Titanium addition can provide these improvements without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
The intended starting high-entropy alloy has a single-phase structure.
The hypothesis should hold for equimolar concentrations of the constituent elements.
The hypothesis should hold when the alloy is made by ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.
Titanium addition causes formation of an ordered B2 bcc phase.
An ordered B2 bcc phase acts as a hard and strong phase in high-entropy alloys.
Formation of the ordered B2 bcc phase enables a load-transfer mechanism.
The load-transfer mechanism associated with the ordered B2 phase increases strength.
The load-transfer mechanism associated with the ordered B2 phase increases hardness.
A titanium-free high-entropy alloy is the untreated baseline.
The titanium amount must be optimized to obtain the desired hardness and strength improvement.
Comparing titanium-containing samples with a titanium-free baseline by nanoindentation and tensile testing can test the proposed hardness and strength changes.

contradictions.description: The conditions require equimolar constituent concentrations, while the intervention, boundary, and experiment require a specific or varying Ti amount. For a fixed set of elements, independently varying Ti makes the alloy non-equimolar unless corresponding composition adjustments are defined.
